where L is the length of the pendulum and g is the acceleration of free fall.
The equation is homogeneous.
What is the value of n?

hints: Notice the base units present: $T$ is measured in $\text{s}$, $L$ in $\text{m}$ and $g$ in $\text{m s}^{-2}$, while $2\pi$ has no units.
Combine $L$ and $g$ first to find the unit of the bracket $L/g$ before applying the power $n$.
Use homogeneity: the power $n$ must turn the unit of $L/g$ into $\text{s}$, so set $(\text{s}^2)^n = \text{s}^1$ and solve for $n$.
walkthrough: Homogeneous means both sides have the same base units. The left side $T$ has unit $\text{s}$.
On the right side $2\pi$ is dimensionless, so the term $(L/g)^n$ must itself have unit $\text{s}$.
Find the unit of $L/g$: $L$ is $\text{m}$ and $g$ is $\text{m s}^{-2}$, so $L/g$ has units $\text{m} / (\text{m s}^{-2}) = \text{s}^2$.
Equate powers of $\text{s}$ with the left side: $2n = 1$, so $n = 1/2$. This is option C.

A.explanation: An exponent of $-2$ would give units of $\text{s}^{-4}$, not the unit $\text{s}$ required for period $T$.

B.explanation: A negative exponent would give $1$ over time, so the right-hand side would decrease when $L/g$ increases and would not have the unit $\text{s}$.

C.explanation: With $n = 1/2$, $(L/g)^n$ has units $(\text{s}^2)^{1/2} = \text{s}$, matching the unit of $T$.

D.explanation: An exponent of $2$ would give units of $\text{s}^4$, which is much larger in base-unit power than the $\text{s}$ needed for $T$.
